sourceRefs.locator: Physical PDF page 1107, printed slide 20; main text and labeled diagram as applicable
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

•  Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a systematic
   graph search algorithm used in robot
   navigation to find a path between two
   points on a graph-based map.
•  Data Structures: It uses a FIFO (First-In,
   First-Out) queue to manage the
   "frontier" (the open set of scheduled
   vertices) and an "explored" set (the
   closed set of visited vertices) to prevent
   backtracking.
•   It ignores the actual weight (distance) on
   the edges, effectively treating all edge
   costs as equal.



                                                                                                          20

sourceRefs.locator: Physical PDF page 1108, printed slide 21; main text and labeled diagram as applicable
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Step-by-Step Execution
•   Initialize:
   –  Frontier: [A]
   – Explored: []
•  Step 1: Expand A. Add its
   neighbors B and C to the frontier.
   –  Frontier: [B, C]
   – Explored: [A]
•  Step 2: Expand the first node in the
   queue, B. Add its unvisited
   neighbors D and E.
   –  Frontier: [C, D, E]
   – Explored: [A, B]

1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Step-by-Step Execution

  neighbor F.

   – Explored: [A, B, C]
•  Step 4: Expand D. Add its unvisited
  neighbor G (the goal).
   – Frontier: [E, F, G]
   – Explored: [A, B, C, D]

sourceRefs.locator: Printed slide 25: Original nine undirected edges and weights
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
2. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)
•  UCS is an optimal graph search algorithm.
   Instead of expanding nodes level-by-level,
    it prioritizes vertices based on the lowest
   cumulative cost from the start vertex.

                Cost: Distance (in km)
•  Mathematical Notation: Minimizes f(v)=g(v),
  where g(v) is the cumulative cost (distance) from the
   start to the current vertex v.
•  Data Structures: It uses a priority queue ordered
   from smallest to largest value of g(v).

sourceRefs.evidenceText:
3. A-Star
•  The A* (A-star) search algorithm is a widely used
   graph search technique in robot navigation that
   finds the optimal path between two points by
   using a heuristic to guide its search.

•  Mathematical Notation: Minimizes f(v)=g(v)+h(v),
   where:
   – g(v) is the path cost from the start to vertex v
      (cost-to-come).
   – h(v) is a heuristic estimating the distance from v
      to the goal (cost-to-go).

sourceRefs.locator: Physical PDF page 1120, printed slide 33; main text and labeled diagram as applicable
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
3. A-Star
•  The performance and accuracy of A* depend critically on the choice of the heuristic
   function:
➢Admissibility: A* is guaranteed to find the lowest-cost path only if the heuristic is
   "admissible," meaning it never overestimates the actual cost of reaching the goal.
  A non-admissible heuristic may lead to a non-optimal path.
➢Common heuristic function Examples:
   – Minimum-Distance: The Euclidean distance is a standard admissible heuristic
      because it is the shortest possible path between two
       points and cannot be an overestimate. (this example)
   – Minimum-Time: The heuristic must represent the travel
      time at the maximum possible speed in the
      environment to remain admissible.


                                                                                                            33

sourceRefs.locator: Printed slide 15: Cardinal cost 1 and diagonal cost square root of 2
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
Representation of environment (Map)

•  While grids and graphs are typically treated as distinct map
   representations, they can be easily converted to allow
   grid-based environments to be searched using standard      4-Connected
   graph algorithms.
•  The conversion process involves placing a vertex in every
   grid cell and adding edges to connect it to reachable
   neighboring cells.
•  Edge Costs based on Connectivity:
                                                                                    8-Connected
   – 4-Connected: Neighbors share an edge (Up, Down,
        Left, Right). Moving to any neighbor has an edge cost
       of 1.0.
   – 8-Connected: Neighbors share an edge or corner
       (adds 4 diagonals). Vertical/horizontal moves cost 1.0,
       diagonal moves cost  2 ≈1.414.


                                                                                                            15

sourceRefs.locator: Printed slide 20: BFS ignores actual edge weight
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

•  Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a systematic
   graph search algorithm used in robot
   navigation to find a path between two
   points on a graph-based map.
•  Data Structures: It uses a FIFO (First-In,
   First-Out) queue to manage the
   "frontier" (the open set of scheduled
   vertices) and an "explored" set (the
   closed set of visited vertices) to prevent
   backtracking.
•   It ignores the actual weight (distance) on
   the edges, effectively treating all edge
   costs as equal.

sourceRefs.locator: Printed slide 24: Weighted routes distinguish geometric distance from hop count
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

•  Pros: Very simple to implement.
   Finds the path with the minimum
  number of transitions/hops (3 hops
  A→B→D→G).

•  Cons: Physically suboptimal.
  Because it ignores road lengths, it
  chooses a longer route (cost of 17)
  over a much shorter alternative
   (cost of 9).

sourceRefs.locator: Lecture L48, physical PDF page 1515, printed footer 9: 16 kHz sampling and 8-bit quantization examples.
sourceRefs.evidenceText:
Stage 1: Digitization
•   Digitization converts speech(analog) into a machine-understandable format(digital)
•  Involves sampling followed by quantization.
   – Step 1: Sampling converts a continuous analog signal into discrete digital
       values by measuring the signal’s amplitude at regular time intervals.
          • Sampling rate (in Hertz) is the number of total samples taken per second
          during digitization. E.g., 16,000 Hz for microphone speech.
          • To accurately measure a sound wave, the sampling rate must be at least
          twice the frequency of the wave.
          • This maximum measurable frequency is known as
          the Nyquist frequency.
    ─  Step 2: Quantization - Once measured, these real-
        valued amplitudes are converted into discrete
        integers (typically 8-bit or 16-bit values).

                                                                                                            9
